**Corporate cards** cost less to run than employee reimbursement for routine, frequent spend, because the company pays the merchant directly and controls the purchase before it happens. Reimbursement still fits rare, small, or unpredictable expenses.


The comparison usually gets framed as cards having fees and reimbursement being free. That's backwards. Reimbursement has no line item on an invoice, so its cost hides in staff hours, in money employees lend the company, and in spending finance learns about weeks after it happened. Once you price those, the question becomes which spend belongs in each model.


***Key Takeaways***


-


With reimbursement, the employee pays first and the company repays later. With a corporate card, the company pays the merchant at the moment of purchase.


-


Reimbursement's costs are staff time per report, employee float, after-the-fact policy review, and late visibility. None appears as a fee.


-


Cards move policy enforcement before the purchase through limits and merchant blocks, while reimbursement can only review a purchase after it's paid.


-


Both models must meet the same IRS substantiation rules, but card data arrives with the merchant, date, and amount already recorded.


-


Reimbursement still makes sense for mileage, new hires without cards, rare spenders, and merchants that don't take cards.


## What's the difference between corporate cards and expense reimbursement?


The difference is who fronts the money and when finance sees the spend. Under reimbursement, the employee pays with personal funds and files a claim. Under a corporate card, the company pays the merchant directly, and the transaction reaches finance within a day or two.


That single difference drives everything else. A reimbursement creates a debt from the company to the employee, which has to be documented, approved, and settled. A card transaction never creates that debt. If you need a refresher on the card side, a primer on[how company credit cards work](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/how-company-credit-cards-work) covers billing, limits, and liability.

## What does each model cost to run?


Reimbursement costs more to run per transaction, because each claim needs an employee to assemble it, a manager to approve it, finance to review it, and a payment to settle it. Cards cut most of those steps, though they bring their own administration.


### How much processing time does each model take?


Each reimbursement claim passes through four or five sets of hands, and each card transaction passes through two or three. The difference is the report itself. With reimbursement, the employee rebuilds the transaction from a receipt, and with a card, the issuer already has it.


The payment at the end of a reimbursement isn't free, either. According to AFP's 2022 Payments Cost Benchmarking Survey, as reported in its[January 2022 release](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/about/learn-more/press-releases/Details/survey-73-of-organizations-are-transitioning-their-business-to-business-payments-from-checks-to-digital-payments) , a check costs a median $2 to $4 to issue and an ACH payment $0.26 to $0.50. Companies that still reimburse by paper check pay the high end every time.


Labor is the larger cost, and it's the one to measure yourself. Time 30 claims from receipt to payment, then 30 card transactions from posting to approval, and multiply each by loaded labor cost. AP teams using Corpay save about 40% of the time they spend on payment processing.


The card side has costs too. Someone has to issue cards, set limits, chase missing receipts, and close cards when people leave. That administration is real, but it's per cardholder rather than per transaction, which is why cards win for people who spend often.


### Who carries the float?


The employee carries the float under reimbursement, lending the company the cost of every purchase until the claim is paid. With a company-paid corporate card, nobody carries it, because the company settles the card statement directly.


For many employees, that's a real burden. According to the Federal Reserve's[report on household economic well-being in 2024](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20250528a.htm) , 63% of adults would cover a $400 emergency expense using cash or its equivalent, which leaves more than a third who wouldn't. A field supervisor who books a week of hotels for a crew can be carrying a few thousand dollars on a personal card. Good employees quietly put off necessary trips because of it, a pattern I've seen often, and that cost never shows up on a finance report.


Liability is part of the float question. On a corporate card, the cardholder's exposure to fraudulent charges is limited by law. Under Regulation Z's[unauthorized-use rules](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/1026.12) , a cardholder's liability is capped at $50 or less. An employee using a personal card for company travel has only their personal card's protections and their employer's promise to repay.


### Where does policy leakage happen?


Policy leakage happens after the purchase under reimbursement, because a reviewer can only reject or question a claim for money that's already spent. Cards move the check before the purchase, so a blocked merchant or an over-limit charge is declined at the point of sale.


Reimbursement review also depends on attention. A manager approving thirty claims on a Friday afternoon checks the totals, not the receipts. Padded mileage, duplicate submissions, and personal items tucked into a hotel folio get through that way, which is why[expense fraud detection](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/expense-fraud-detection-prevention) leans so heavily on after-the-fact audits for out-of-pocket claims.


Cards still need review, but the work shifts from reading receipts to setting[card controls and spend policies](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/card-controls-spend-policies) once and watching the exceptions. There's no reliable public figure for how much spend leaks under either model, so measure your own. Pull a sample of last quarter's approved claims, re-review them against policy, and count what slipped through.


## When does finance see the spend?


Finance sees card spend within a day or two of the purchase, and reimbursed spend only when the employee submits the claim. That gap is often weeks, and it matters most at month-end, when unsubmitted expenses become accruals someone has to estimate.


The delay compounds. An employee who travels late in the month may not submit until the following month, and a manager who's traveling too may not approve for another week. Finance closes the books with a guess. With cards, the transaction exists before the receipt does, so there's far less unsubmitted spend to estimate, though charges that haven't posted or synced to the ERP by the close still need an accrual. Matching receipts to transactions becomes the work, and[corporate card reconciliation](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/corporate-card-reconciliation) is far easier to automate than reimbursement review.


Speed of data also changes budget conversations. A department head who can see this week's card spend can stop a problem mid-month. One who learns about it from expense reports finds out next month. Corpay connects card data to the ERP through more than 100 ERP integrations, including NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Business Central, and Acumatica, so transactions post with their coding already attached.


## How do tax and receipt rules differ?


The tax and receipt rules are the same for both models in substance, since the IRS cares whether an expense is substantiated and has a business purpose, not how it was paid. The practical difference is that card transactions arrive with the merchant, date, and amount already recorded.


For reimbursements, the accountable plan rules decide whether repayment is tax-free to the employee. Under[IRS Publication 463](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p463) , accounting for expenses within 60 days and returning any excess within 120 days are safe harbors that count as a reasonable time. They aren't hard deadlines, and missing them doesn't automatically make a reimbursement taxable, but reimbursements paid under a plan that fails the accountable plan requirements are treated as wages. The[employee expense reimbursement guide](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/employee-expense-reimbursement) walks through those rules in detail.


Receipt thresholds apply to both. The same IRS publication doesn't require documentary evidence for expenses other than lodging under $75, though many company policies ask for receipts on everything. Card data doesn't replace a receipt for IRS purposes, but it does give you a record of the amount, date, and merchant without depending on a crumpled paper slip.


## When does reimbursement still make sense?


Reimbursement still makes sense for spend you can't reasonably put on a company card, such as personal-vehicle mileage, purchases by employees who spend only a few times a year, new hires before their card arrives, and merchants that don't accept cards.


Mileage is the clearest case. There's no merchant to pay, so it will always be a[reimbursable expense](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/reimbursable-expenses) calculated from a log. Rare spenders are the next. Issuing and managing a card for someone who expenses two lunches a year costs more than processing the two claims.


The federal government shows where the default lands at scale. Under the Federal Travel Regulation,[41 CFR 301-51.1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/41/301-51.1) requires federal employees to use the government's contractor-issued travel charge card for all official travel expenses unless an exception applies. Reimbursement stays as the exception path, which is roughly the right shape for a company too.


## How do you decide which model fits your company?


Decide by sorting employees by how often they spend and what they buy, then putting frequent spenders on cards and leaving occasional spend in reimbursement. Most mid-market companies end up running both, with cards as the default.


Four questions settle most cases:


-


How many times a month does this person or role spend company money?


-


Is the spend predictable enough to set merchant categories and limits?


-


Do the merchants they use accept cards?


-


Can finance absorb the administration of issuing and managing more cards?


If the answers point to frequent, predictable spend at card-accepting merchants, a card is the cheaper model. If they point to rare or unpredictable spend, reimbursement is. A company with dozens of[employee credit cards](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/employee-credit-cards) and almost no reimbursement left is usually a well-run one.


My position is that reimbursement should be the exception path, and most companies still run it as the default. Where it stays, it should be fast, and[expense reimbursement software](https://www.corpay.com/resources/blog/expense-reimbursement-software) can make the remaining claims cheaper to process. What no tool settles is the cultural part. Some employees like using their own card for the points, and taking that away is a conversation, not a policy memo.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is a corporate card better than expense reimbursement?


For frequent, predictable spend, a corporate card is usually better, because it removes the expense report, the employee float, and the delay before finance sees the charge. For rare or small expenses, mileage, and merchants that don't take cards, reimbursement remains the simpler choice.


### What is the ROI of switching from reimbursement to corporate cards?


The return comes mainly from processing time saved on every claim that no longer exists, plus earlier visibility and fewer policy exceptions. Rebates on card spend add a smaller return. Measure your current cost per expense report to estimate it for your company.


### What are the benefits of corporate cards for mid-market companies?


Mid-market companies gain controls that act before a purchase, transaction data that reaches finance within days, fewer expense reports to process, and no employee float on company-paid cards. Card programs also earn rebates that reimbursement never does.


### Can employees use a corporate card for personal expenses?


Most corporate card policies prohibit personal use. Where an accidental personal charge happens, the policy should require the employee to report and repay it promptly, and the program administrator should review repeated cases as a policy violation.


### Do corporate card charges need receipts?


Yes, in most cases. Card data records the merchant, date, and amount, but the IRS still expects substantiation of business purpose, and many company policies require a receipt for every charge. Receipt capture at the point of purchase makes this easier than collecting paper later.
